What is a tense in English?

Great question! A tense tells us when an action happens. There are three main tenses. The present tense is for what happens now or every day: 'Amina eats rice.' The past tense is for what already happened: 'Amina ate rice yesterday.' The future tense is for what will happen later: 'Amina will eat rice tomorrow.' See how the verb 'eat' changes to 'ate' and 'will eat'? The verb carries the time of the action. Listen for tenses when people speak at home and school. You are doing very well!

How do I form the past tense of a verb?

Well done for asking! For most verbs, we add -ed to form the past tense: walk becomes walked, play becomes played, and jump becomes jumped. So we say, 'Yesterday, Chidi walked to school.' But some verbs are special and change completely; we call them irregular verbs. Go becomes went, eat becomes ate, see becomes saw, and come becomes came. There is no -ed for these, so we must learn them by heart. Practise by telling a friend three things you did yesterday. Keep it up, you are learning fast!

How do I talk about the future in English?

Good question! To talk about the future, we use 'will' or 'shall' before the verb, or 'is going to'. For example: 'I will visit my grandmother in the village next week.' 'We shall write a test on Friday.' 'Ngozi is going to wash the plates after dinner.' Notice that the main verb does not change; 'will' does the work of showing future time. Words like tomorrow, next week and later often appear with the future tense. Try saying three things you will do this weekend. Excellent effort!

What is the difference between 'go', 'goes', 'went' and 'will go'?

Lovely question! All four come from the same verb, 'go', but they show different times and persons. We say 'I go to school' and 'they go to school', but 'she goes to school', because with he, she or it we add -es in the present tense. 'Went' is the past tense: 'Emeka went to Kano last month.' 'Will go' is the future: 'Emeka will go to Kano next month.' So the time of the action and the person doing it decide which form to use. Make your own sentences with each form. Well done!

Is this sentence correct: 'Yesterday I eat beans'?

Good try, but the sentence is not correct. The word 'yesterday' tells us the action already happened, so we need the past tense of 'eat', which is 'ate'. The correct sentence is: 'Yesterday I ate beans.' Remember, 'eat' is an irregular verb, so we do not say 'eated'. Here are more examples: 'Yesterday I ate rice and stew,' and 'Last week we ate moi-moi at the party.' Always match the time word with the verb form. You spotted a common mistake many pupils make, so well done for checking!

What is the present continuous tense?

Great question! The present continuous tense describes an action happening right now, at this very moment. We form it with 'is', 'am' or 'are' plus a verb ending in -ing. For example: 'I am reading my book.' 'Mama is cooking jollof rice.' 'The pupils are singing the national anthem.' Compare it with the simple present: 'Mama cooks every day' talks about a habit, but 'Mama is cooking now' talks about this moment. Look around you and say what people are doing right now using -ing verbs. You are improving every day!

Can you give me examples of irregular verbs and their past tense?

Of course! Irregular verbs change completely in the past tense instead of adding -ed. Here are common ones: go becomes went, eat becomes ate, see becomes saw, come becomes came, take becomes took, give becomes gave, run becomes ran, sing becomes sang, write becomes wrote, and buy becomes bought. For example: 'Halima bought bananas at Mile 12 market,' and 'The choir sang beautifully on Sunday.' The best way to learn them is to use them in your own sentences every day. Pick five today and make a sentence with each. Keep practising!

Rewrite this sentence in the future tense: 'Ada visits her aunty in Enugu.'

Let us do it together! The sentence 'Ada visits her aunty in Enugu' is in the present tense. To change it to the future tense, we put 'will' before the verb and use the base form of the verb: 'Ada will visit her aunty in Enugu.' Notice that 'visits' loses its -s and becomes 'visit', because after 'will' we always use the plain verb. We can add a time word to make it clearer: 'Ada will visit her aunty in Enugu next Saturday.' Now try changing 'Musa plays football' to the future. Well done!
